pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: For each of these, say stack or queue and defend the choice: undo in an editor, jobs sent to a printer, the browser back button, keystrokes waiting to be processed.
expected_points: undo and back button are stacks: the most recent action must come out first
printer jobs and keystroke buffers are queues: arrival order must be preserved
the deciding question is whether removal should return the newest or the oldest element

questions.prompt: What should Pop or Dequeue do when the container is empty, and how does Peek differ from Pop? How did your implementation signal the empty case?
expected_points: empty removal must be signaled, not panic — the comma-ok (value, bool) convention, like a map lookup
Peek returns the same element Pop would but leaves the container unchanged
callers check ok before trusting the value

questions.prompt: Compare a slice-backed and a linked-node queue: what goes wrong when you dequeue from the front of a slice, and what does the linked version cost you instead?
expected_points: shifting elements on each dequeue is O(n), so draining n elements is O(n^2)
reslicing items[1:] is O(1) time but keeps the backing array reachable, pinning memory the queue will never read again
linked nodes with head and tail give true O(1) at both ends and let dequeued nodes be garbage-collected
the linked version pays an allocation per element and loses cache-friendly contiguity

questions.prompt: A push onto a slice-backed stack sometimes copies every element into a bigger array. Why do we still describe push as O(1)?
expected_points: growth doubles capacity, so expensive copies are rare and get rarer
total copy work across n pushes is O(n), so the average per push is constant
this averaged figure is called amortized O(1); individual pushes can still be slow

questions.prompt: Walk through how your Balanced decides that "([)]" is unbalanced. Why can't a simple open-minus-close counter do this job?
expected_points: openers are pushed; each closer pops and must pair with the popped opener
on ')' the pop returns '[', which does not pair, so the answer is false
a counter only tracks how many are open, not which opener was most recent — nesting is LIFO, so a stack is required
a leftover non-empty stack at the end also means unbalanced

questions.prompt: Name two real systems built around queues and explain why FIFO is the right discipline for each.
expected_points: task scheduling (print jobs, background jobs): first submitted, first served is the fairness contract
buffering (keystrokes, packets, audio): producer and consumer run at different speeds and order must survive the handoff
breadth-first search processes vertices in discovery order, which is exactly FIFO

questions.prompt: Design puzzle: build a queue out of two stacks. How does it work, and what is the amortized cost of dequeue?
expected_points: enqueue pushes onto an in-stack; dequeue pops from an out-stack, refilling it by draining the in-stack when empty
each element is moved at most twice, so dequeue is amortized O(1) even though a single refill is O(n)
